desc:
Inventory forecasting from past sales tells you what to reorder, how much and when. Ecom Swift LLC studies your sales history, seasons and supplier lead times, then builds a simple forecast in a sheet you own, with notes on how each figure is worked out.

## What is inventory forecasting?

Inventory forecasting is an estimate of how many units of each product you will sell in the coming weeks, based on how they sold before. From that estimate you can work out how many days of stock remain and when a new order must be placed so goods arrive before shelves empty.

A forecast is not a promise. It is a disciplined guess that replaces gut feeling with your own numbers. For a small store, that is often the difference between reordering in time and apologizing for backorders.

## Why stock planning decides your cash and your sales

Stock problems come in two kinds, and both cost money. Running out of a bestseller means lost sales, disappointed customers and ad spend that sends traffic to a page with nothing to buy. Overbuying slow products ties up cash in boxes that sit in a store room, and discounting them later cuts into margin.

Most owners manage this by feel: a quick look at the stock count and a memory of last winter. That works for a dozen products and fails at a few hundred. A forecast gives each product its own rate of sale, so attention goes first to the items that will run short soonest and away from the ones that can wait.

## What a useful forecast includes

- Expected sales per product for the coming period, based on your actual order history.
- Days of stock left, calculated from the current count and the expected rate of sale.
- Seasonal patterns, such as a winter coat that sells in autumn and barely moves in summer.
- Supplier lead times, so the reorder date accounts for production and shipping.
- A suggested order quantity that covers demand until the next delivery.
- A low stock list that puts the most urgent products at the top.
- Variants and sizes forecast separately, because a medium and an extra large rarely sell alike.
- A slow and dead stock view that shows what has stopped moving.
- A cash figure for the next order, so you know what to set aside.
- A plain notes tab explaining each formula in words.

## How we build it

We start with a sales export from your store, ideally covering a full year so seasons are visible. We also ask for current stock counts and each supplier's usual lead time and minimum order size.

We clean the data first. Out of stock periods can look like low demand, and one large wholesale order can look like a trend, so we mark and adjust these cases and tell you what we changed. Then we build the forecast sheet so every number traces back to a source you can read.

The Basic package covers your top selling products with days of stock left and a simple reorder list. The Standard package adds seasonal patterns, supplier lead times, suggested order sizes and a low stock list. The Premium package forecasts variants, adds the slow stock view and the cash needed for the next order, and gives you a short guide so you can refresh the sheet yourself every month. If you sell on more than one channel, we combine the orders into one view.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Update stock counts before using the forecast.
- Add a safety margin for suppliers who are often late.
- Mark planned promotions, because they distort normal sales.
- Review the sheet each month and compare it with real sales.
- Order in larger batches only when the supplier terms really save money.

**Avoid:**
- Treating the forecast as exact.
- Reordering a product just because it sold well once.
- Ignoring variants, which hides size and color shortages.
- Forgetting lead times when choosing a reorder date.
- Keeping dead stock in the plan, which makes the whole sheet look healthier than it is.

## Who this is for

It suits a store owner who sells a few hundred items and keeps running out of the best ones. It suits a seasonal seller who needs to decide how much to buy before the peak. It also suits a team that reorders by memory today and wants a written plan another person can follow.

## What we need from you

Send an export of your orders, your current stock counts and a list of suppliers with their lead times and order minimums. Tell us about past stockouts or promotions that skewed sales. We never need passwords: an exported file is enough, and if you prefer a live connection, access is given as a collaborator, staff or developer user with limited permissions.
